did_you_know.text: Did you know? In the psalm’s title, it is called “A Song, a Psalm of Asaph”—both a song and a psalm—and is attributed to Asaph.
Did you know? The psalm opens with three parallel pleas for God not to remain silent: “Do not keep silent,” “Do not hold Your peace,” and “Do not be still.”
Did you know? The enemies are described as conspiring and consulting together against “Your hidden ones”—a designation for those whom God protects or shelters.
Did you know? The enemies’ goal is stated in extreme terms: to destroy Israel so that its name as a people would no longer be remembered.
Did you know? The psalm lists a long line of nations and groups joining forces against Israel, including Edom, the Ishmaelites, Moab, and the Hagrites.
Did you know? Assyria is described as joining Israel’s enemies and serving as an “arm” for the descendants of Lot—that is, Moab and Ammon.
Did you know? The psalmist asks God to act against the enemies as He did in the past against Midian, Sisera, and Jabin, whose defeat is associated here with the Kishon River.
Did you know? En-dor is mentioned as the place where the enemies were destroyed, and the image of “dung on the ground” emphasizes their humiliation and defeat.
Did you know? The enemies are compared to a whirling dust storm and to chaff scattered by the wind; later, images of fire, flame, tempest, and storm also depict the power of divine judgment.
Did you know? The psalm concludes by stating its purpose: that everyone may know that You alone, whose name is the LORD, are Most High over all the earth.
